reasons: The formula text is descriptive and is not checked against the calculator here.
The part percentages are not checked to add up to one hundred percent.
No test is visible for these shapes.
The optional median and the success flag are not enforced by this file.

terms.meaning: a defined shape that says which fields a piece of data must or may have.
a field that may be left empty.
a way to give each new object its own fresh copy of a default list, so objects do not share one list.
a class built on another class that inherits its fields and adds its own.
minimum sustainable price, the lowest price a seller can accept and stay in business.
market median price, the typical price in the market.
a cost measured per kilowatt of direct current capacity of the panels.
net present value, the value today of future yearly payments after discounting.
the middle value between a low and a high value.
the step-by-step teaching explanation of how each cost was reached.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Setup of imports
sections.what: Brings in the tools needed to define the shapes, including lists, optional values, and pydantic base types.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond what the classes below need.

sections.name: CostRange
sections.title: Low, high, and middle value
sections.what: Holds a low value, a high value, and an optional middle value. A method can fill the middle value with the average of the low and high values.
sections.why: Likely reason: many costs are ranges, so the low and high ends are stored together.
sections.watch_out: The middle value stays empty until the calculate_median method is called.

sections.name: ComponentCost
sections.title: Shared base for cost items
sections.what: Defines the common shape for every cost item: a minimum sustainable price range, a market median price range, a formula text, an optional list of parts, and a unit label that defaults to dollars per kilowatt DC.
sections.why: Likely reason: every cost item shares these fields, so they are defined once here.
sections.watch_out: Both price ranges are required, so a cost item missing either one will fail validation.

sections.name: ModulesOutput
sections.title: Module cost output
sections.what: Describes the module cost with its own formula text and a default split into material, labor, and logistics at 65, 25, and 10 percent.
sections.why: Likely reason: the module cost has its own formula and parts, so it gets its own shape.
sections.watch_out: The split is a fixed default in this file, and nothing checks it against the real cost breakdown.

sections.name: InvertersOutput
sections.title: Inverter cost output
sections.what: Describes the inverter cost with its formula text and a default split of equipment at 75 percent and installation at 25 percent.
sections.why: Likely reason: the inverter has its own formula and parts, so it gets its own shape.
sections.watch_out: The formula text names only the minimum inverter price, while the output has both a minimum and a maximum. Check the calculator to see which is really used.

sections.name: ESSOutput
sections.title: Battery storage cost output
sections.what: Describes the battery cost with its formula text and a default split across cells, management electronics, enclosure, and installation.
sections.why: Likely reason: the battery is optional, so its shape is kept separate and marked optional elsewhere.
sections.watch_out: The battery formula text divides by system size right after multiplying by it, so the intent is unclear. The calculator is the place to confirm the real math.

sections.name: SBOSOutput
sections.title: Racking and tracker cost output
sections.what: Describes the structural balance of system cost. Its formula text chooses between the tracker price and the fixed racking price, and its default split covers racking, tracker motors, and foundations.
sections.why: Likely reason: the racking cost depends on whether a tracker is used, so the formula picks the right price.
sections.watch_out: The formula text uses only a single minimum price for each option, which may not match the range shown in the output.

sections.name: EBOSOutput
sections.title: Electrical balance of system cost output
sections.what: Describes the electrical balance of system cost with its formula text and six default parts covering transformers, breakers, combiners, wiring, shipping, and tariffs.
sections.why: Likely reason: electrical costs are many small items, so they are split into parts.
sections.watch_out: As written in the formula text, the shipping and tariff multipliers seem to apply only to the wiring term, not to the whole sum. Check the calculator for the real order.

sections.name: FieldworkOutput
sections.title: Field labor cost output
sections.what: Describes the on-site labor cost with its formula text and a default split across installation, electrical work, and commissioning.
sections.why: Likely reason: field labor is its own category with its own hours and rates.
sections.watch_out: The formula depends on the labor burden rate, so a change to that rate changes this cost too.

sections.name: OfficeworkOutput
sections.title: Office labor cost output
sections.what: Describes the office and soft-cost labor with its formula text and a default split across engineering, permitting, project management, and legal.
sections.why: Likely reason: office work is costed separately from field work, so it gets its own shape.
sections.watch_out: The formula relies on input names matching the input file exactly. A renamed input would break this formula.

sections.name: OtherOutput
sections.title: Other costs output
sections.what: Describes the taxes, contingency, overhead, and profit added on top of the earlier costs, with its formula text and a default split across those four items.
sections.why: Likely reason: these allowances are added on top of the subtotal, so they come after the other cost items.
sections.watch_out: The formula sums a range of items by their position, so the order in which items appear in the export affects the total. The calculator should be checked to confirm this.

sections.name: OMOutput
sections.title: Yearly operations and maintenance output
sections.what: Describes the operations and maintenance cost, expressed as a present value over twenty years, with its formula text and a default split across six items.
sections.why: Likely reason: running costs continue for years, so they are discounted to a value today.
sections.watch_out: The twenty-year period is written into the formula text, so changing the plant life elsewhere would not update this text.

sections.name: SystemTotal
sections.title: System total shape
sections.what: Describes a system-level total, with a low and high range, its formula text, and a default unit of dollars per kilowatt DC.
sections.why: Likely reason: the grand total needs the same range and unit fields as the parts.
sections.watch_out: The total's low and high values are not linked to the parts in this file, so they must be kept consistent by the calculator.

sections.name: CostModelOutputs
sections.title: Complete output for one run
sections.what: Gathers every cost item, the totals with and without battery storage, the time of calculation, and the session code into one result. Battery items are optional, so they may be missing when storage is off.
sections.why: Likely reason: one structure holds the whole answer for a single run.
sections.watch_out: The battery total can be empty when storage is off, so code that reads it must allow for that.

sections.name: ValidationResult
sections.title: Validation message shape
sections.what: Describes a single message about an input or output, with a field name, a status, a message, a severity, and optional suggested fixes.
sections.why: Likely reason: messages need the same structure so the front end can show them consistently.
sections.watch_out: The status and severity are free text, so nothing limits them to the words named in the descriptions.

sections.name: WebResearchSource
sections.title: Web research source shape
sections.what: Describes one cited source, with a title, web address, quoted excerpt, relevance score from zero to one, and timestamp.
sections.why: Likely reason: each finding should show where it came from so a user can check it.
sections.watch_out: The web address is stored as plain text and is not checked to be a working address.

sections.name: WebResearchResult
sections.title: Web research result shape
sections.what: Describes the research findings for one component, including checks on inputs and outputs, suggestions, quoted notes, sources, and a confidence value that defaults to 0.8.
sections.why: Likely reason: research results need a common shape so they can be shown and saved the same way.
sections.watch_out: The default confidence of 0.8 is a fixed number, not something measured, so it should not be read as proof of accuracy.

sections.name: CalculationStep
sections.title: One teaching step shape
sections.what: Describes one step in the lecture, with a step number, title, component, visual state, plain explanation, formula text, worked example, parts, context, and optional research.
sections.why: Likely reason: each lecture step must carry everything the front end needs to show it.
sections.watch_out: The visual state and explanation are free-form, so the front end must be ready for any content.

sections.name: LectureSequence
sections.title: Full lecture sequence shape
sections.what: Describes the ordered list of teaching steps with a total count, the current step, and a completion percentage from zero to one hundred.
sections.why: Likely reason: the front end needs the step list and its progress together.
sections.watch_out: The total step count is stored separately from the list, and nothing checks that the two agree.

sections.name: ErrorDetail
sections.title: Structured error shape
sections.what: Describes an error with a code, a type, a message, an optional field name, an optional suggested fix, and a severity.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed shape makes errors easier for the front end to show.
sections.watch_out: The visible code in the backend main file does not use this shape. Its errors are plain messages instead, so this shape may be unused.

sections.name: ModelResponse
sections.title: Overall API response shape
sections.what: Wraps everything a calculation returns: a success flag, the outputs, validation messages, research, lecture, errors, warnings, and extra metadata. The calculate endpoint returns this shape.
sections.why: Likely reason: one wrapper gives callers a single, consistent response format.
sections.watch_out: The success flag and the data field are not forced to agree, so a response can say success while data is missing, or the reverse.

summary: Defines the shape of every result the calculator returns, including cost ranges, cost parts, totals, research notes, teaching steps, and the overall response.
purpose: Gives every result a fixed structure so the API, the Excel export, and the front end all know what to expect.
why: Likely reason: a shared structure makes results predictable. Some formula text is stored here to document how each number is built. The file does not state the reasons more fully.
how: CostRange holds a low value, a high value, and an optional middle value. ComponentCost is the shared base for each cost item and holds its price ranges, its formula text, its unit, and an optional list of parts. Each cost type builds on that base and sets its own formula text and default split across parts. Totals and the overall response are assembled from these pieces.
inputs: Values created by the calculator code. The formula text is descriptive and is stored as plain text, not run as calculation here.
outputs: Validated output objects that are returned by the API or written into the Excel export.
risks: The formula text is documentation only and could drift away from the real math in the calculator. The middle value stays empty unless the calculate_median method is called. The part percentages are not checked to add to one hundred percent, although every default set currently does. The success flag and the data field are not forced to agree.
debug: If a result fails validation, compare the field names used by the calculator with the names in this file. If a median is missing, check that calculate_median was called. If a formula looks wrong, compare it with the calculator code, since this file does not run it. If a split looks off, add the percentages for that item.
